title: Carney says vote on controversial bill to fast-track projects will be whipped for Liberal MPs
summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says all Liberal MPs are expected to vote in favour of Bill C-39, the government's controversial legislation designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney rises during question period on Wednesday. He said on Friday that he expects all Liberal MPs to vote for Bill C-39. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney says all Liberal MPs are expected to vote in favour of Bill C-39, the government's controversial legislation designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and re-write labour laws — securing its passage through the House of Commons.
Bill C-39 is headed to a third reading vote in the House of Commons

Prime Minister Mark Carney says all Liberal MPs are expected to vote in favour of Bill C-39, the government's controversial legislation designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and rewrite labour laws — securing its passage through the House of Commons.

The sweeping piece of legislation, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, is meant to fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of "national interest" to preapprove certain types of projects. To do so the bill would overhaul some environmental rules and other regulations to expedite construction.
The legislation is a key piece of the government's promise to build energy and infrastructure projects — like mines, ports and pipelines — in the face of the trade dispute with the United States.
But the bill has raised concerns among labour advocates and environmentalists — and grumblings from from within Carney's caucus.

blocks.text: Asked Friday if the vote on Bill C-39 will be whipped, Carney called it the most important piece of economic legislation his government has put forward.
"You're a member of the party and so, we will vote as a government," he said during a news conference in Yellowknife.
Unlike a free vote, where members vote according to their own conscience, a whipped vote means all caucus members must vote with the party's position or face discipline.
Making it a whipped vote all but guarantees Bill C-39's passage in the House, where the Liberals hold a 173-seat majority.
There have been signs not everyone in Carney's caucus is happy with the bill, which besides rolling back environmental regulations would would also make changes to collective bargaining.

Last month, Vancouver MP Patrick Weiler called for more guardrails in the bill. Earlier this week another B.C. Liberal, Will Greaves, aired his concerns publicly, writing in an opinion piece in the Toronto Star that he is "worried" Canada is losing its climate credibility.
A day before Carney confirmed the vote would be whipped, his House leader, Steven MacKinnon, told CTV News he was confident the legislation would pass without needing to do so.
"I don't think we have to whip the vote," MacKinnon said. "We're very, very proud to be able to hold this bill up as an example of the great things we can get done for our country."

Despite voting in favour previously, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre announced Thursday his party will vote against C-39 after a special committee studying the bill only made minor amendments. The Bloc and NDP also oppose the bill.
